topic: Finger sprains and jams in ball sports

slides.headline: Jammed a finger catching the ball?
slides.sub: Why tugging it straight isn't the move, and what helps instead.

slides.title: Skip the tug-it-back trick
slides.body: Pulling on a jammed finger can stress the same ligaments that just got sprained. Instead, step off the court, cool it with a wrapped cold pack and keep your hand raised for a while.

slides.title: Buddy taping: the useful bit
slides.body: Taping the sore finger to its neighbour gives support while still letting it bend. Put a little padding between the fingers, keep the tape snug rather than tight, and redo it if the skin gets irritated.

slides.title: Keep the other joints moving
slides.body: Gently bending the knuckles you can move, plus making a loose fist a few times an hour, usually stops the whole hand stiffening up. Some puffiness around a finger joint can linger for weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A fingertip that won't straighten on its own, a joint that looks bent or out of place, numbness, big swelling or trouble gripping a cup are worth an assessment soon, as some need early splinting.

slides.title: Easing back into the game
slides.body: Most people return with tape on first. Test the finger with gripping, pinching and easy catching drills before a full game. Cricket, netball and beach volleyball season all put fingers in the firing line.

slides.headline: Finger still puffy and stiff?

topic: Quads cooked after leg day: massage and recovery

slides.headline: Leg day left your quads cooked?
slides.sub: What massage can and can't do for next-day thigh soreness.

slides.title: That ache has a name
slides.body: Delayed onset muscle soreness usually peaks one to two days after unfamiliar or heavier training, like new squat variations or walking lunges. It's a normal response to load, not a sign you've hurt yourself.

slides.title: Where massage fits
slides.body: Research suggests massage can ease how sore you feel and help you move more comfortably for a while. It won't dramatically speed up muscle repair, and it doesn't replace sleep, food or sensible programming.

slides.title: Keep moving, gently
slides.body: An easy walk, a light spin on the bike or some bodyweight squats through a comfortable range often helps more than lying on the couch. Gentle movement tends to take the edge off stiff quads.

slides.title: Plan the next leg day
slides.body: Soreness is usually worst after a jump in volume or a brand new exercise. Add sets gradually, leave a couple of reps in the tank, and the same session often feels far easier within a few weeks.

slides.title: When it's more than DOMS
slides.body: Sharp pain during a lift, sudden swelling or bruising, or very dark urine with severe muscle pain after extreme exercise need a GP or physio check rather than a massage.

topic: Reformer terms explained: springs, footbar and carriage

slides.headline: New to the reformer? Learn the lingo
slides.sub: Carriage, springs, footbar, straps and headrest, in plain English.

slides.title: The carriage: the bit that moves
slides.body: The padded platform you lie, kneel or sit on is the carriage. It slides along rails, and your job is usually to control it on the way out and, just as importantly, on the way back in.

slides.title: Springs: heavier isn't always harder
slides.body: Springs add resistance, but heavier springs can make some exercises easier by giving you more support. Lighter springs often ask for more control. Your instructor chooses them to suit your body and goals.

slides.title: The footbar: your base
slides.body: The padded bar at the end is where your feet or hands push. It can usually be raised or lowered. Heels, arches or toes on the bar change which muscles work the hardest.

slides.title: Straps, headrest and shoulder rests
slides.body: Straps connect your hands or feet to the springs for pulling and leg work. The headrest adjusts for neck comfort, and shoulder rests stop you sliding off the end during pushing exercises.

slides.title: Getting on and off safely
slides.body: Check the carriage is still and the springs are secure before you climb on or off, and ask your instructor to show you how. Moving slowly and with control is part of the exercise too.

slides.body: Our clinical Pilates team starts with an assessment, then shows you around the reformer at a pace that suits you. Book online, link in bio.

topic: Stiff, sore big toe (hallux rigidus)

slides.headline: Big toe stiff when you push off?
slides.sub: A stiff big toe is common, and there's plenty you can do about it.

slides.title: Why the big toe matters
slides.body: Every step, your big toe bends as you roll through to push off. When that joint gets stiff and sore, walking, running, squatting and rising onto your toes can all feel harder than usual.

slides.title: What's usually going on
slides.body: Hallux rigidus is a common arthritis-related stiffening of the big toe joint, sometimes with a bony bump on top. It tends to build over years, and symptoms usually go up and down with load.

slides.title: Shoes can take the load off
slides.body: A stiffer sole or a gentle rocker shape lets you roll through without bending the toe as much. Thongs and very bendy sneakers often feel worse, which is handy to know heading into summer.

slides.title: Keep the foot strong
slides.body: Calf raises within a comfortable range, toe and arch exercises, and general leg strength can help you walk with less strain on the joint. Your physio can adjust the range and volume as it settles.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A toe that's hot, red and very swollen, pain that wakes you at night, numbness, or a sudden change after an injury are worth an assessment rather than waiting it out.

topic: Self-massage with a ball: a 5-minute routine

slides.headline: Got a tennis ball? You've got a routine
slides.sub: Five minutes, four spots, one ball. Handy between massage appointments.

slides.title: Minute 1: feet
slides.body: Stand and roll the sole of one foot over the ball from heel to toes with gentle pressure, about thirty seconds each side. A nice reset for feet after long days in shoes or thongs.

slides.title: Minute 2: calves
slides.body: Sit on the floor with the ball under one calf. Slowly roll or rest on tender spots while pointing and flexing your foot. Cross the other leg on top if you want a bit more pressure.

slides.title: Minute 3: glutes
slides.body: Sit on the ball on one side and lean into the fleshy part of your buttock, making small slow circles. Move off anything that feels sharp or sends tingling down the leg.

slides.title: Minutes 4 and 5: upper back
slides.body: Stand with the ball between a shoulder blade and a wall. Lean in and move slowly around the muscles beside the spine, staying off the bony spine itself and away from the front of the neck.

slides.title: Keep it comfortable
slides.body: Aim for pressure around 4 to 6 out of 10 that eases as you go. Skip areas with bruising, varicose veins, a recent injury or numbness, and stop if symptoms start spreading.

slides.headline: Want help with the tricky spots?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists can work the areas a ball can't reach and suggest what to roll at home between visits. Book online, link in bio.

caption:
All you need for this five-minute routine is a tennis ball and a wall.

Start with the soles of your feet, then calves, then glutes, and finish with two minutes on the upper back against a wall. Go slowly, breathe out, and keep the pressure moderate. It should ease as you go, not build.

Self-massage is a nice way to take the edge off tightness between appointments. It won't replace movement or strength work, but it can make both feel a bit easier.

topic: Choosing a mattress: what actually matters

slides.headline: Mattress shopping? What actually matters
slides.sub: Firm or soft? The answer is more personal than the ads suggest.

slides.title: Medium-firm is a starting point
slides.body: Research suggests a medium-firm mattress suits many people with back pain better than a very firm one. It's a starting point rather than a rule. How you feel when you wake up matters most.

slides.title: Match it to how you sleep
slides.body: Side sleepers often like a bit more give at the shoulder and hip. Back and stomach sleepers usually prefer a little more support. Couples may need a compromise, or a split-firmness option.

slides.title: Test it properly
slides.body: Lie on it for 10 to 15 minutes in your usual sleeping position, not 30 seconds in the showroom. If a trial period is offered, check the conditions carefully before you commit.

slides.title: The mattress isn't everything
slides.body: Pillow height, room temperature, stress and how active you were that day all affect morning stiffness. On a hot Sydney summer night, a cooler room can matter as much as new foam.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain that's worse at night whatever position you're in, pain with fever or unexplained weight loss, or numbness or weakness in the legs deserve an assessment, not another mattress.

topic: Clicking or clunking hip: when it matters

slides.headline: Hip clunks when you move?
slides.sub: Most clicks are harmless noise. Here's how to tell when it matters.

slides.title: Noise alone is usually fine
slides.body: Plenty of hips click or clunk during leg raises, squats or getting out of the car. If it doesn't hurt and you can move normally, it's usually just a tendon sliding over bone.

slides.title: Common harmless culprits
slides.body: A band of tissue flicking over the bony point on the side of the hip, or the hip flexor tendon at the front, are frequent sources. Dancers and gym-goers notice these a lot.

slides.title: Clicking plus pain is different
slides.body: Clicking with a deep, catching pain in the groin, a sense of the hip locking or giving way, or pain that builds with sitting can point to a joint issue that's worth assessing.

slides.title: What usually helps
slides.body: Strengthening the glutes, hip flexors and trunk, and adjusting the movements that provoke it, can often reduce painful clicking. Chasing the noise with stretching alone rarely changes much.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A hip that locks, pain that stops you walking normally, pain after a fall, or groin pain with fever deserve a prompt assessment rather than more stretching.

topic: Keeping a simple pain diary

slides.headline: Can't remember what set it off?
slides.sub: A simple pain diary helps you and your practitioner spot patterns.

slides.title: Keep it short
slides.body: One line a day is enough: a pain score out of 10, what you did, how you slept and anything that helped. A notes app on your phone works fine. You're after patterns, not a novel.

slides.title: Track activity, not just pain
slides.body: Write down walks, gym sessions, long drives or big desk days. Pain often lags a day behind, so seeing Tuesday's gardening next to Wednesday's flare-up can be really useful.

slides.title: Note the wins too
slides.body: Record what went well, like a longer walk, a pain-light morning or a full night's sleep. Progress can feel slow when you only notice bad days, and the wins help your team adjust the plan.

slides.title: Look at weeks, not days
slides.body: One rough day doesn't mean you're going backwards. Look over a week or two. Is it easier in the morning? Worse after sitting? Linked to stress or poor sleep? That's the useful stuff.

slides.title: Bring it to your appointment
slides.body: A quick scroll through your diary gives your physio, chiropractor or massage therapist much more to work with than 'it's been up and down'. It helps each session feel more focused.

topic: Massage for older adults: what to know

slides.body: Skin and tissues can bruise more easily as we get older, and firmer doesn't have to mean more effective. Many older clients find moderate pressure feels great and still eases stiffness.

slides.body: Lying face down isn't comfortable for everyone. Side-lying, extra pillows or a seated position are all options. Getting on and off the table slowly and with support is part of the session too.

slides.body: Massage can ease stiffness and feel relaxing, but staying strong and steady on your feet comes from regular movement. Walking, strength work and balance practice are the long-term partners.

topic: Pain on the outside of the ankle (peroneal tendons)

slides.headline: Ache along the outside of your ankle?
slides.sub: Often the peroneal tendons. Here's what usually helps them settle.

slides.title: Meet the peroneals
slides.body: These two tendons run behind the bony bump on the outside of your ankle. They help steady your foot, especially on uneven ground, trails and sand, and when you change direction quickly.

slides.title: Why they get cranky
slides.body: Often it's a jump in load: more running, a new trail, long beach walks in soft sand or a lingering ankle sprain. Feet that tend to roll outward can add extra strain as well.

slides.title: Settle, then strengthen
slides.body: Ease back on whatever flared it without stopping everything. Then build up with band exercises turning the foot outward, calf raises and balance work. Tendons usually respond well to gradual, steady loading.

slides.title: Check your footwear
slides.body: Worn-out shoes or very soft, unstable sneakers can make things worse. A supportive, well-fitting shoe for walking and training is a good starting point while it settles.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A clicking or snapping feeling behind the ankle bone, swelling that doesn't ease, an ankle that keeps giving way, or pain after a bad roll deserve an assessment.

topic: What 'neutral spine' means (and doesn't)

slides.headline: Neutral spine isn't a pose to hold
slides.sub: What your Pilates instructor actually means, and why it isn't rigid.

slides.title: It's a range, not a point
slides.body: Neutral spine is simply a position where your spine's natural curves are present, not flattened or exaggerated. It differs between people, and there's a comfortable zone rather than one exact spot.

slides.title: Why we use it in Pilates
slides.body: Starting from neutral gives you a consistent reference, so you can feel what your trunk, hips and shoulders are doing. It's a teaching tool for control, not a rule for everyday life.

slides.title: What it doesn't mean
slides.body: It doesn't mean your spine should never bend or twist. Healthy backs flex, round and rotate all day long. Plenty of Pilates exercises deliberately move you out of neutral, and that's the point.

slides.title: Find yours in 30 seconds
slides.body: Lie on your back with knees bent. Gently tip your pelvis to flatten your lower back, then arch it. Settle about halfway, with a small gap under your lower back. That's roughly neutral.

slides.title: Easy on the bracing
slides.body: Holding neutral shouldn't mean clenching your stomach and holding your breath. Light, steady effort and relaxed breathing usually work better and make the exercises feel smoother.

slides.headline: Curious what neutral feels like?
slides.body: Our clinical Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy starts with an assessment and coaches you through it on the mat or reformer. Book online, link in bio.

topic: Floor play with kids: easier on your back

slides.headline: Down on the floor with the kids?
slides.sub: Small tweaks that make playtime easier on your back and knees.

slides.title: Change position often
slides.body: Kneeling, side-sitting, cross-legged, lying on your tummy: rotate every few minutes. Backs rarely mind any one position for a while. What they tend to mind is the same one for an hour.

slides.title: Bring the play up a level
slides.body: Puzzles, blocks and colouring can happen at a coffee table or on a couch cushion. You still get the time together without folding in half for the whole session.

slides.title: Getting up off the floor
slides.body: Roll onto your side, come up onto hands and knees, step one foot forward and push up through your legs. Using a couch or chair for a hand is smart, not lazy.

slides.title: Lifting little ones
slides.body: Get close before you lift, bend at the hips and knees and let your legs share the work. If your back is feeling sore, turning your feet rather than twisting at the waist often feels easier.

slides.title: Build your floor strength
slides.body: Squats, lunges and getting down to the floor and up again a few times a day keep you capable. School holidays with the kids at home are a good time to practise.

topic: Hip replacement: what the first 12 weeks look like

slides.headline: Life after hip replacement, week by week
slides.sub: Every surgeon's protocol differs. This is a general picture, not your plan.

slides.title: Weeks 1 to 2: getting moving
slides.body: Most people are up and walking with an aid soon after surgery. Short, frequent walks, the exercises from the hospital team and following your surgeon's precautions are the main jobs.

slides.title: Weeks 2 to 6: building routine
slides.body: Walking distance usually grows, and exercises often progress towards more standing strength and balance work. Swelling and tiredness are common. Your surgeon's advice on movement limits and driving comes first.

slides.title: Weeks 6 to 12: getting stronger
slides.body: Many people rely less on walking aids and build hip and leg strength more steadily. Stairs, longer walks and everyday tasks often feel easier, though progress varies a lot between people.

slides.title: Everyone's timeline differs
slides.body: Age, fitness before surgery, other health conditions and the surgical approach all affect recovery. Comparing yourself with a friend or neighbour rarely helps. Steady, gradual progress is the aim.

slides.title: When to call your surgeon or GP
slides.body: Increasing redness, warmth or discharge around the wound, fever, new calf pain or swelling, or a sudden change in how the hip feels need prompt medical advice. Chest pain or breathlessness needs urgent care.

topic: Massage for hikers' legs

slides.headline: Big bushwalk, wobbly legs the next day?
slides.sub: Where massage helps hikers recover, and where it doesn't.

slides.title: Downhill is the hard part
slides.body: Walking downhill asks your quads and calves to brake with every step. That's why soreness is often worst after the descent, especially on long stair sections like those on Sydney's coastal walks.

slides.title: Where massage can help
slides.body: A remedial massage a day or two later can ease tightness in the calves, quads, hips and feet and help you move more comfortably. Research suggests it mainly helps how sore you feel.

slides.title: What massage won't do
slides.body: It won't make up for a big jump in distance or elevation. Training on hills and stairs in the weeks beforehand usually does more to reduce next-day soreness than anything afterwards.

slides.title: Recovery on the day
slides.body: Drink plenty of water, especially in summer heat, eat a decent meal and take an easy walk the next morning. Sitting still for hours on the drive home often leaves legs stiffer.

slides.title: When it's not just sore legs
slides.body: Sharp pain in one spot, swelling in a calf, pain that worsens rather than eases after a few days, or a knee or ankle that won't take weight needs a physio or GP check.

topic: Pilates for hikers

slides.headline: Train for the trail on the reformer
slides.sub: How Pilates builds the balance and control that hills and rocky tracks ask for.

slides.title: Single-leg strength matters
slides.body: Every step on a trail is a small single-leg balance exercise. Pilates work like single-leg footwork, reformer lunges and side-lying series builds strength one leg at a time.

slides.title: Control on the way down
slides.body: Downhills need your quads and glutes to work while they lengthen. Slow, controlled returns of the carriage train that braking skill, which can make long descents feel more manageable.

slides.title: Ankles that react
slides.body: Balance work, heel raises and footwork on the footbar can help your ankles adjust to rocks and tree roots. Many people notice steadier footing after a few weeks of regular practice.

slides.title: A trunk that carries a pack
slides.body: A day pack adds load to your back and shoulders. Exercises for the trunk, upper back and hips help you carry it comfortably for hours without slumping over by lunch.

slides.title: Plan your build-up
slides.body: Two sessions a week alongside regular walks on hills and stairs is a practical starting point. Start several weeks before a big hike, rather than the week before, so your body can adapt.

topic: Front-of-shoulder pain (biceps tendon)

slides.headline: Ache at the front of your shoulder?
slides.sub: The biceps tendon is a common source. Here's how it's usually managed.

slides.title: Where the biceps tendon lives
slides.body: The long head of the biceps runs up the front of your shoulder through a groove in the upper arm bone. When it's irritated, pain often sits right at the front and can travel down the arm.

slides.title: What tends to flare it
slides.body: Lots of overhead lifting, chin-ups, bench press, carrying heavy bags or a sudden jump in training. It often shows up alongside other shoulder issues, like an irritated rotator cuff.

slides.title: Adjust, don't stop
slides.body: Ease back on the lifts that provoke it for a while, like wide-grip bench or deep dips, and keep training everything else. Complete rest usually slows things down rather than speeding them up.

slides.title: Rebuild the load
slides.body: Gradual strengthening for the biceps, rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles is usually the core of rehab. Your physio can guide how quickly to add weight, range and speed.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A sudden pop with bruising down the arm, a new bulge in the upper arm, weakness bending the elbow, or night pain that isn't settling deserve an assessment.

slides.headline: Shoulder pinching at the front?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your shoulder and training, then map out a plan that keeps you lifting. Book online, link in bio.

caption:
That nagging ache right at the front of your shoulder during bench or chin-ups? The biceps tendon is often involved.

It tends to flare with a jump in overhead or pressing work, heavy carrying, or alongside other shoulder niggles. Most people don't need to stop training. Easing back on the lifts that provoke it while keeping everything else going usually works better than full rest.

From there, gradual strengthening for the biceps, rotator cuff and shoulder blade muscles does the heavy lifting.

A sudden pop with bruising or a new bulge in the arm is worth getting checked.

topic: What your massage therapist is feeling for

slides.headline: What are those hands actually checking?
slides.sub: What your remedial massage therapist is feeling for during a session.

slides.title: Texture and tone
slides.body: Therapists feel whether muscles are soft, firm or guarded, often comparing one side with the other. It's a guide to where to spend time, not proof that something is wrong.

slides.title: Tender spots
slides.body: Sensitive, knotty-feeling spots are common and often ease with steady pressure. Your feedback matters here, because tenderness partly reflects how sensitive your nervous system is that day.

slides.title: How you react
slides.body: Tensing up, holding your breath or pulling away tells your therapist to ease off. Good massage works with your body, so speaking up about pressure is always welcome.

slides.title: Warmth and swelling
slides.body: Areas that feel warm, puffy or unusually sensitive can be a reason to go gently, work elsewhere or suggest you see a physio or GP before more massage.

slides.title: It's not a diagnosis
slides.body: What a therapist feels is useful information, but it doesn't replace a proper assessment. If something needs further checking, they'll suggest seeing a physio, chiropractor or your GP.

topic: Getting in and out of the car all day: back care for drivers

slides.headline: In and out of the car all day?
slides.sub: Couriers, tradies and reps: small habits that make a long driving day easier.

slides.title: Sit first, then swing
slides.body: Getting in, sit on the seat with your feet still outside, then turn your knees and legs in together. Reverse it to get out. It spares your back the twist-and-duck.

slides.title: Set the seat up once
slides.body: Seat close enough to reach the pedals with a slight knee bend, backrest fairly upright rather than reclined, and a small lumbar support if it feels better. Worth checking in any new vehicle.

slides.title: Use every stop
slides.body: Each time you get out, take ten seconds: stand tall, lean back gently, walk a few steps. Short, frequent movement breaks add up over a long day behind the wheel.

slides.title: Lifting from the boot
slides.body: Slide the load close to the edge of the boot before lifting, keep it near your body and use your legs. A crate or step to raise heavy items can make a big difference.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain with numbness in the legs or saddle area, new bladder or bowel changes, or pain that keeps getting worse despite rest deserve prompt medical attention.

slides.headline: Driving all day for work?
slides.body: Our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy assess your back and daily routine, and combine hands-on care with practical exercises. Book online, link in bio.

caption:
Forty stops a day and your back feels every single one?

Set your seat up once so you're not reaching for the pedals, and use each stop for ten seconds of standing tall and a few steps.

When lifting from the boot, slide the load close first and use your legs.

Numbness in the legs or saddle area, or bladder changes, need prompt medical attention.

topic: ACL injury: the first few weeks

slides.headline: Heard a pop and your knee gave way?
slides.sub: What the first few weeks after an ACL injury often look like.

slides.title: Get it assessed early
slides.body: A pop, fast swelling and a knee that feels unstable are worth a physio or GP assessment soon after. Early testing helps work out what's been injured and what the next steps are.

slides.title: Settle the swelling
slides.body: In the first days, relative rest, ice, compression, elevation and crutches if needed help calm things down. Gentle movement within comfort usually starts early rather than waiting weeks.

slides.title: Get the knee straight again
slides.body: Getting the knee fully straight and the quads switching on are early priorities. Simple exercises like quad sets and heel slides often start within days, guided by your physio.

slides.title: Surgery or rehab first?
slides.body: Current guidelines suggest not everyone needs a reconstruction, and some people do well with structured rehab. It depends on your goals, sport and knee, and is a shared decision with your surgeon and physio.

slides.title: Keep the rest of you moving
slides.body: Upper body work, the other leg and stationary cycling when it's comfortable help keep your fitness and spirits up. The first weeks are about calm, steady progress, not testing the knee.

slides.headline: Just hurt your knee?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your knee, guide the first weeks and liaise with your GP or surgeon if needed. Book online, link in bio.

topic: Why we ask about sleep, stress and work

slides.headline: Why we ask about more than your back
slides.sub: Sleep, stress and work shape how pain behaves. Here's why they matter.

slides.title: Sleep changes pain sensitivity
slides.body: Research suggests poor sleep can make the nervous system more sensitive, so the same activity may hurt more after a bad night. That's useful to know when planning your exercises and load.

slides.title: Stress turns up the volume
slides.body: Busy seasons, deadlines and big life changes can raise muscle tension and make pain feel louder. It's not 'all in your head'. It's how the body and brain work together.

slides.title: Work shapes the daily load
slides.body: Hours at a desk, driving, lifting or standing all change what your body handles each day. Knowing your routine helps us suggest exercises and changes that fit real life.

slides.title: It shapes your plan
slides.body: If sleep is patchy or work is flat out, we might start with shorter exercises, adjust expectations or build in more movement breaks. The plan is built around you, not a template.

slides.title: Share what you're comfortable with
slides.body: You never have to share more than you want to. Even a rough picture helps, and if something falls outside what we do, we'll suggest checking in with your GP.

slides.body: Heart conditions, blood pressure changes, a history of blood clots or medications that affect clotting all change how firm the pressure should be and which areas are worked.

slides.title: Recent injuries or surgery
slides.body: Fresh sprains, strains, fractures, recent operations or new scars need care around the area. Your therapist may work around it, adjust the approach or suggest seeing a physio first.

slides.title: Pregnancy
slides.body: Pregnancy changes positioning and technique, and some areas are worked more gently. Let your therapist know how many weeks along you are and any advice from your midwife, obstetrician or GP.

topic: Back to sport after ACL reconstruction: why it takes time

slides.headline: ACL rehab: why patience pays off
slides.sub: Feeling good isn't the same as ready. Here's what return to sport involves.

slides.title: The graft needs time
slides.body: A new ACL graft keeps remodelling for many months after surgery. The knee can feel fine well before it's ready for cutting, jumping and contact. Your surgeon's protocol sets the early boundaries.

slides.title: Strength before speed
slides.body: Quad and hamstring strength often lag behind for longer than people expect. Rehab usually builds strength first, then running, then jumping and landing, then change of direction.

slides.title: Testing, not guessing
slides.body: Rather than a date on the calendar, return decisions often use strength tests, hop tests and sport-specific drills compared with the other leg. Confidence in the knee matters too.

slides.title: Why rushing rarely pays
slides.body: Research suggests returning to pivoting sport too early is linked with a higher chance of reinjury. A longer, well-planned build-up is usually a better bet than a quick comeback.

slides.title: Keep the motivation going
slides.body: Set small goals, track your strength numbers and train with your team where it's appropriate. Many people find the mental side of the comeback as big as the physical side.

slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios work alongside your surgeon's protocol, with testing to guide each step back to sport. Book online, link in bio.

That's why return decisions usually rely on strength and hop testing and sport-specific drills rather than a date on the calendar, always alongside your surgeon's protocol. Research suggests a patient build-up lowers the chance of reinjury.
